utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just remind you, sir, that you took a -- made a declaration yesterday to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. You are still bound by that declaration today, to tell the truth. Okay? Thank you very much. Mr. Milovancevic, two questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. Thank you, Your Honours. Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Medakovic, yesterday, at one point you mentioned that you learned about the number of people who had arrived from Zagreb, that there were 200 of them who had arrived in trucks and with weapons, from Vlado Vukovic who had been captured. My question is: What was his occupation, and was he mistreated in order to acquire that information?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, in my evidence, I mentioned that this group, in passing through Glibodolski Kriz, captured our guards. On the following day, we severed off the roads leading from Saborsko to Slunj in order to collect prisoners for exchange. We didn't want our nine people to remain in Saborsko for a long period of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, the question is: What was his occupation, and was he mistreated? Can you just deal with that, please. What was his occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a policeman in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was he mistreated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He was brought to Plaski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: You gave an answer to my question as to whether he was mistreated but you were interrupted. Were you going to say anything else?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was going to say that following the exchange, the group who had captured Vlado Vukovic and two other Croatian policemen brought them to Plaski. Vlado Vukovic spent a night in Plaski. He wasn't mistreated. He was even invited to attend a birthday party of the man who captured him.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The second question I'm going to put to you is: Did you write a letter to Rudolf Spehar; and if so, when and why?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Following the completion of the operation to leave the siege, or rather after the operation on Saborsko, on the 13th of November, I wrote a letter to Rudolf Spehar and I sent it via civilians who expressed a desire to go to Ogulin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: And in my question I also asked you why.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said in my evidence earlier that I had talked to Rudolf Spehar several times. He was president of Ogulin municipality. I also felt a need to explain to him what had happened in Saborsko and why.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence has completed its examination-in-chief. Thank you. Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic. Mr. Whiting, yesterday you wanted to raise an issue during the middle of the examination-in-chief. I asked you if you could hold it back. Would you like to raise it at this point, before you start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, from my point of view, there is no need to raise it now. We can raise it -- I'm ready -- I'm prepared to start my cross and go forward. It is an issue -- it's a serious issue and it's an issue that we think bears on future witnesses, and I'm happy to raise it when this witness is finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. It is actually the most appropriate moment to do it at that time, but I thought you were in a hurry to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I was. No longer. I'm fine to proceed, Your Honour. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Medakovic. Is it Medakovic or Medakovic? How do you pronounce your name?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Medakovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will do my best. My name is Alex Whiting. I'm one of the Prosecutors in this case. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Before I ask any questions, I have to send an e-mail to the Defence, which I have now done. Sir, can you tell me when you were first interviewed by the Defence of Milan Martic? And when I say that, I mean when you were first interviewed by an investigator, by lawyers for Mr. Martic. When were you first contacted?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date, but I think it was in September and it was through the investigator, Mr. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: September of what year, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This year, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were contacted for the first time in September of 2006? That's the first time you spoke with somebody from the Defence of Milan Martic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Maybe it was late August, but certainly not earlier than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How was that contact made? Were you called on the phone? Were you met in person?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first contact was made on the phone with Mr. Radivoj Nikolic, and then we met in person.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you met in person, were you interviewed? Did he interview you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I actually remembered, I apologise, that he had called me earlier on the phone. I think it was in July. Yes, in July he called me on the phone for the first time, and then the first meeting we had was in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that's July of 2006?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By the way, when is the last time you spoke with Milan Martic, himself?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's hard to say. I can't remember the date, but certainly while we were still in Krajina. I've never seen him in Serbia, except when I saw him at the airport, when he was on his way here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Were you at the airport on that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the group of people seeing him off. I wasn't alone there. There was a group of people, so I doubt that he saw me. But I saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was approximately May of 2002; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date. I know it was several years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It was in 2002; correct? You can't remember that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, but I can't be sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you tell us why you went to the airport that day?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have known Mr. Martic for a long time and I have great respect for him, as a man. I consider him my friend. And I felt it my duty to see my president off, just like other people from Krajina did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you still consider him your president?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Even to this day?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's go back to your interviews with the Defence. You say you were interviewed in August of 19 -- or sorry, August of 2006. Was that interview recorded?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I sent a fax to Mr. Nikolic. I sent it from the company where I worked at the time, and it was a statement that I wrote by myself. I wrote my personal particulars there - date of birth, education - and then what I did during the war. I wrote it in my own hand. My handwriting is rather bad. And it was two pages long. Following that, we spoke in his office, and then we met once in Novi Sad. And that was all as far as our contacts are concerned. Then I saw him once again, just prior to coming here when he gave me my passport and my visa, because he was doing that for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, if you could listen carefully to my question and answer my question. When you met with the Defence investigator, was the conversation recorded?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say. I didn't notice that it was being recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The statement that you wrote, the two-page statement that you wrote and faxed, did you sign it? Was it signed by you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not sure I understand your answer. You think so? We're talking about August of 2006, which, by my count, is some two or three months ago. Do you not remember if you signed it or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote it by my own hand and I sent it by fax, since I work in Novisad and Mr. Nikolic was in Belgrade. And that was in July. Most likely I signed it, just like I sign other documents. I think I did sign it, but I hesitate with my answer because I'm not fully sure and I don't want to make a mistake. It is certain, though, that it was in my own handwriting. Nobody else wrote it but me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Are you having trouble remembering these events that happened in July of 2006? Because you've been testifying here about events that occurred in 1990/1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I tried to remember important events. I don't see the writing of a statement and whether I signed it as something so important that requires me to remember it. This contained only my personal particulars. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When you were interviewed in August of 19 -- sorry, August of 2006, you say you don't know if it was recorded. Was any statement written out that you signed or read over containing the information that you provided?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Whiting, didn't the witness say he was interviewed in September?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I thought he said August, but maybe I'm -- well I can ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, did you say you were interviewed in August or September of 2006, when you met in person with the Defence investigator in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was in September, maybe in August. I don't remember the exact date, but it was definitely late August or early September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, when you were interviewed, was a statement taken? Was the information written down and did you review the information? Did you sign anything?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did look over my statement. It had two typed pages with my particulars, what I did during the war, when I came to Serbia, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, it also talked about these events that you've testified about, didn't it? What happened in Plaski, what happened in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It said that I was involved in negotiations; correct. It was an abbreviated version of what I said in my evidence yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this is the second time you've come to The Hague, isn't it? You were here some two weeks ago, nearly three weeks ago, for testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you came here that first time to testify, did you meet with Defence counsel, Mr. Milovancevic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And did you talk about your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did you review documents?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reviewed my statement, and I think that I saw some other documents, two or three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, sir, when you met with Mr. Milovancevic on that occasion and you went over your testimony, you told him everything that you have told the Court here yesterday; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, approximately so. Whenever you start talking of a topic, things start coming back to you. These things didn't take place two or three years ago but many more years ago. And yesterday, for example, I made a mistake in the first name of one of the two Susnar men. I apologise to the Trial Chamber, but it just occurred to me later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I don't recall. Did you have an opportunity to correct that mistake or do you want to correct that mistake now?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to correct it now. I made a mistake in the first name. The last name was correct, but I made a mistake in the first name.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And why don't you make that correction. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When talking of the event at Glibodolski Kriz, I said that Susnar Milan, Susnar Bogdan and Petrovic Bogdan died. The name of the other Susnar person is Stevo. I erroneously said his first name was Bogdan and I apologise to the Trial Chamber for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, going back to my question, is it fair to say that, aside from a few details, all the important matters that you told the Trial Chamber about yesterday were things that you had told the Defence about in your previous meetings; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, I want to put a -- I'm going to put a series of statements to you, sir, because I want you to know, from the very start, what our position is concerning your testimony. Do you follow me? Do you follow what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Because our position is that you have turned reality on its head. Do you follow what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My position is that you are trying to do that yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I see, sir. Just listen to my question and answer my question. Do you follow what I'm saying? Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand what you're saying, but I disagree with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I understand. Now, with respect to each of these statements, I'm just going to ask you to tell me if you disagree or you agree with the statement. We don't need to have explanation or anything more. Just tell me if you agree or disagree, and we'll get into more details later. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After August of 1990 and into early 1991, barricades were erected in the Serb villages around Saborsko, including in Plaski, Licka Jesenica and Plitvice. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not around Saborsko. Barricades we're erected in all areas, not around Saborsko, but also in the direction of Ogulin and another place.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the other place.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I disagree with you that this was in Saborsko and around it, in the surrounding villages. Plaski is not a village, it's a town. And all other places are villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will put the question to you. I will rephrase it, then. Barricades in 1990, after August, 1990, were erected in Plaski, in Licka Jesenica and Plitvice. Agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak of Plitvice. I know that during that period of time, during a brief period of time, there were barricades which were removed later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Those barricades in Plaski and Licka Jesenica stayed up through 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, when do you say they came down?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The events in Knin are well known. On the 17th of August, 1990. And this --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, let me interrupt you, because if you don't listen to my questions and just answer my questions, we're going to be here for a very, very long time, because we have a lot of ground to cover. So, please, when do you say the barricades in Plaski and Licka Jesenica came down? If you could just answer that question.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was there only for a brief period of time and it was in 1990. In 1991, there were no longer barricades. It lasted for a mere 15 days or so, in August of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After the barricades came down, they were replaced by police checkpoints; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. What police checkpoints are you referring to? Which villages? Which period of time? Which locations? This is a very general question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The same villages that you are talking about, sir. The same villages where you say the barricades came down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yesterday I said accurately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry. Just answer the question. When did the barricades -- after the barricades came down, did police checkpoints -- were police checkpoints mounted; yes or no? We haven't got much time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, didn't you testify yesterday - and it's at page 37 of the transcript yesterday - that there was -- on July 22nd of 1991, there was a checkpoint at Vojinovac, which is located between Plaski and Josipdol. Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember, and that's true. But you asked me about something quite different. We are now speaking of 1990, and you are skipping over six months in the future and referring to a time when there was a combat between Josipdol and Vojinovac. That's when the unit for special purposes had already been formed. That's what you are referring to. So you basically went forward a year, and it's very difficult for me to follow what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You're doing just fine. Can you tell me when the police checkpoints were erected around Plaski?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the return of the group of people I had taken to Knin for training, we occasionally carried out checks of the vehicles passing through our territory. On the 22nd of July --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on our side --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- I'm going to interrupt you, because you told us yesterday you took the men for training in May of 1991. So is it your testimony, sir, that from approximately September of 1990 until May of 1991, there were no barricades, no checkpoints, no defensive positions at all around Plaski? Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were some village guards, but nothing was organised --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- on my side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: -- get caught up here too much in terminology, okay? When I ask about barricades or checkpoints, in my mind that would include village guards. When were the village guards set up? Were they set up after the barricades were taken down in August 1990, August or September of 1990?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One might say that. They occasionally cropped up. In places where people had hunting weapons, they organised themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you're telling us that this was spontaneous and not commanded in any way; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In early 1991, as I said, I was conducting negotiations in the Croatian parliament. Had I been organising such things, they probably wouldn't have allowed me to go there. You must have information about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, you weren't the only person in Plaski at the time, were you? I mean, there were others who could have organised these village guards; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said they were self-organised in villages and hamlets. People stood guard, but there were no physical obstacles on the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You testified already that Plaski separated itself from the Republic of Croatia and it joined the SAO Krajina in January of 1991; first, as a part of Titova Korenica municipality and then as its own municipality, Plaski. Correct? You agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're twisting what I said, yet again. I said that the first referendum for joining the Krajina was held as early as August 1990. In 1991, there was a referendum for the separation of the local communes from Bugojno municipality and their accession to the Korenica municipality. That's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So Plaski joined the SAO Krajina in August of 1990; that's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: From January of 1991, the SAO Krajina did not recognise the authority of the Croatian Ministry of Interior within the SAO Krajina; agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know from what date, but I know that around that time they stopped recognising the authority, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: By April of 1991, the villages of Saborsko, Vukovici and Poljanak were surrounded on both sides by Serb forces; Plaski on one side and Plitvice on the other side. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were surrounded by the Serb population. I don't know what forces you're talking about at that time. Are you referring to some sort of armed forces? What units are you referring to? If you're referring to forces, you might be precise. There were no forces and no units at that time. There were just eight policemen in Plaski. I don't know how many there were in Korenica and Plitvice.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's move ahead in time. Let's say by the summer of 1991, you would agree with me, would you not, that there were Serb forces, meaning police units, TO, and JNA, in both Plaski and in Plitvice, on both sides of these villages of Saborsko, Vukovici and Poljanak.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, in the summer, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In the summer of 1991, more precisely in August of 1991, the Serb forces began shelling the villages of Saborsko and Poljanak. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you about Saborsko, but Poljanak could not be shelled from the area I was responsible for, because it's more than 30 kilometres away from Licka Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you can tell us that Saborsko was shelled starting in August of 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke about this yesterday. I said that, from the direction of Borik, farmers going about their business in the fields were targeted and we had to respond to these provocations. When we responded, the provocations stopped. I spoke about this yesterday, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So answer is yes, Saborsko was shelled by Serb forces.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to be precise, yet again. What forces and with what? We didn't have shells at the time. Shells or ammunition used in guns, cannons, we didn't have those.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, what did you target Saborsko with, then?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think several mortar mines of 82 millimetres were fired on their positions in the areas of Borik and Sivnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When this started to occur in August of 1991, civilians in those villages - or we'll just talk about Saborsko since you cannot talk about Poljanak - civilians in Saborsko started to leave the village, and those who remained in the village stayed in the village, did not travel about. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't know that precisely because I didn't go into Saborsko at that time. But I heard that some women and children had already started moving out at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In September, October and November of 1991, men from Saborsko were arrested by Serb forces and Martic's police. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have mentioned three months here. I agree about September. I started speaking about that twice, but His Honour interrupted me. If you want, I will clarify who was arrested, and when.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, that answer is sufficient. Thank you. Civilians, even before November 12th of 1991, civilians were killed in Saborsko in September, October or November of 1991. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The men who were arrested from Saborsko were detained and they were beaten. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is a lie launched here by Vlade Vukovic. I saw that in the transcript of the Milosevic trial. It's a blatant lie.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't ask you to comment on another witness's testimony. I just asked you if you agree or disagree. And if you would please listen to my questions and just answer my questions.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We captured enemy soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree that they were maltreated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were imprisoned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. In November of 1991, the villages of Saborsko, Poljanak, and Vukovici were attacked. The remaining civilians who were there were either killed or driven out, and those three villages were destroyed. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, we spoke about that military operation for two hours here. You have reduced it to two sentences. I cannot agree with the way you describe it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: One of the reasons for the attack on these villages was to join the Serb territory of Plaski with the rest of the SAO Krajina. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reason was to make possible normal communications with the rest of SAO Krajina, to lift the siege of Plaski, the entire municipality, not just the town and, of course, the military facilities of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: During the attacks on Poljanak, Lipovaca, Vukovici and Saborsko, crimes were committed against Croat civilians in those villages. Do you agree or disagree? And if you can only speak about Saborsko, just tell us.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I ask you again not to put questions to me about Poljanak and Lipovaca. They were on a completely different axis and I know nothing about them. Yesterday, I described all the events in Saborsko and abide by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Excuse me. It is the prerogative of the Prosecutor to ask you questions about any subject. If you don't know anything about the subject he asks you about, you say you don't know. It's not for you to tell him what questions he may or may not ask, okay? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I will limit the question to Saborsko. Could you just answer the question: Crimes were committed -- during the attack on Saborsko on the 12th of November 1991, crimes were committed against civilians in Saborsko. Do you agree or disagree? Don't think about what you testified about yesterday. Just please answer my question.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit I commanded and I personally committed no crimes. I have not seen those crimes and I cannot talk about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But you heard about them, didn't you? You know about them, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard about them and I received reports, after the sanitization of the terrain, about civilians who had been killed, women and elderly men.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And these crimes were not isolated events in these villages, but they were systematic and widespread. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree. That's your construction.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The purpose of these crimes was to ensure that Croats would leave these villages and never return. Do you agree or disagree, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And finally, sir, whatever the reason was for the attack on these villages, there was no justification for these crimes on the civilians. Do you agree or disagree?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A crime can never be justified.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's talk about your position now. You testified that, in May of 1991, you went with a group of men to Golubic for training and that you returned to Plaski. Those men who were trained in Golubic formed a special purpose unit; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You were in charge of the special purpose unit.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The special purpose unit was within the Ministry of the Interior; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're referring to the Ministry of the Interior of the SAO Krajina, then, yes, one might say that. But you have to put the question more clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for that clarification. When you say "one might say that," the answer is, yes, it was within the Ministry of the Interior of the SAO Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, were you subordinated to Dusan Latas or were you directly subordinated to Milan Martic, as head of the special purpose unit?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dusan Latas was not my superior, but we cooperated well. He had other tasks. I considered Mr. Martic to be my commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was true of all the special purpose units, wasn't it? They were directly subordinated to Mr. Martic; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak about other units. I can only speak about the one I commanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you wore the patch of the SAO Krajina police; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Either on my left or my right sleeve, I don't remember which, there was a semi-circular patch with the words "Milicija Krajina," Krajina police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can we see Exhibit 266, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, while we're waiting, could I ask a question in the interim. Why did you consider Mr. Martic your commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time, he was the Minister of the Interior of the SAO Krajina. That's how we referred to him. I don't know whether there were any documents to that effect, but we considered him to be the Minister of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And therefore?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. He was the commander. We were subordinate to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Who would that "we" include? When you say "we," to whom are you referring, other than you, yourself, in your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm referring to me personally and the unit I commanded, which had some two platoons, about 40 men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just -- just one question on this point. Did you receive your instructions directly from Mr. Martic for whatever?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of the geographical distance, we rarely communicated. For the most part, I had to rely on myself and make decisions myself. These decisions pertained only to the narrow area I was in charge of. My contacts with him happened in Knin, and that was only on one or two occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, listen to my question. Whether it was once, twice, or a million times, did you receive your instructions directly from Mr. Martic; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now we see Exhibit 266 on the screen. Is that the patch that you wore when you were the commander of the special purpose unit after May of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the patch.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. You testified yesterday that the SAO Krajina police - and I understood that to be the police under the command of Dusan Latas - had the job of policing, and that the duty of the special purpose unit was to "materialise the will of the people" and to protect Plaski. So is it fair to say that the special purpose unit had essentially a military function, correct, as opposed to a traditional policing function?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can hardly say that a unit consisting of 40 men can have some sort of serious military function.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I didn't ask you whether it was serious or not. I just asked you what its function was. Its function was, it was a military function as opposed to traditional policing, which was left to the regular police; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was special-purpose policing: Preventing the incursion of terrorist groups, controlling roads, securing important facilities such as waterworks, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Until when were you the commander of the special purpose unit?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the time the Territorial Defence brigade was established in Plaski. I think it was the 1st of September. I'm not sure about the date, but I'm sure it was in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Was it, then, Rade Milanovic who became the commander of the special purpose unit of the police?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some of the men from that unit did not agree to become part of the Territorial Defence brigade, and they did not meet the conditions to enter the police force, so he commanded a group on his own, which never had more than 15 to 20 men. But in the end they became subsumed under other units.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's take this one step at a time. When he commanded this group of men, it was still the special purpose unit that you had commanded starting in May of 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not that unit. It was a group of men who were renegades, who would not obey me personally. They felt they were better than the territorials. It was a group of adventurers, led by another adventurer, Rade Milanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Did Rade Milanovic have a role in the attack on Saborsko on the 12th of November, 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rade Milanovic never played any role in any offensive or defensive action. All he did was strut around in uniform. I think he wasn't even in Plaski when the attack on Saborsko occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's go back to September of 1991. The special purpose unit of the SAO Krajina police continued to exist in September, October, November of 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at Exhibit 607. This is a handwritten order dated the 10th of November, 1991, from Bogdan Grba, and he was your superior in the TO; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only in the Saborsko operation. At that time I was already president of the municipality. I had no military duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's look at page 2 of the document, and it's also page 2 in the English. I just have to orient -- on the English it's the top half, and on the B/C/S it's at the bottom. Do you see where it says, "Special Purposes Unit 1 Company Police and Reserve Police, the unit is commanded by Nikola Medakovic." Now, that's a reference to special purpose unit of the SAO Krajina police; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Grba made a mistake here. He mentions a unit which did not exist. The other two parts are in correspondence, the actual --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, do you see the text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it's your testimony that Mr. Grba, in November of 1991, referred to a unit that, according to your testimony, did not exist and had not existed since September of 1991. Is that your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That former unit, apart from the renegade part with Rade Milanovic, entered the composition of the regular and reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Isn't it, in fact, the case, sir, that you, in your testimony, are trying to eliminate the existence of the special purpose unit in November of 1991? Isn't that, in fact, what's happening here?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm giving first-hand evidence, sir, because I established that unit and disbanded it, so I know about the time of its existence. People used to refer to this unit as Martic's men, and this term was in use until 1995. Whoever saw that unit in 1991 referred to them as Martic's men, and maybe they were part of another unit at the time. That's how it was. That's the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's look at Exhibit 605, then, please. This is -- 605 is a report written by Dusan Latas, the commander of the regular police in Plaski on the 23rd of November, 1991. And I draw your attention - it's on page 1 - to the bottom half of the page. There is a paragraph that begins, "On the 8th --" keep going down, please, on the B/C/S. "On the 8th of November --"

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have the English? Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: There's a paragraph which begins: "On the 8th of November, 1991, our unit was given the task to retake the Glibodol cross." And then the next paragraph, it says: "For this task, we received reinforcements of a special purpose unit from Plaski, comprising about 15 men, while the Plaski DB section acted directly with our unit." You're not saying that Dusan Latas also made the same mistake, are you? In fact, there was a special purpose unit in Plaski in the police in November of 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you show me the entire document so that I can read it and see what it's about? Based on this segment alone, I can't draw proper conclusions. You pull things out of the context and I only see a portion of the document. Who was this sent to? By whom? When?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you can look at the top. We've cut off the very top of the document now. There we go. It's a report from the Plaski police station on the 23rd of November, 1991, and it's about events that had occurred during the previous reporting period. And there's a reference -- he makes a reference to being reinforced by the special purpose unit from Plaski, and that is the special purpose unit of the SAO Krajina police. Correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just scroll down, please, so that I can see the entire text. This is an event that I, described yesterday, the retaking of Glibodolski Kriz. I took part in it, too, not as a unit commander but as a volunteer. And there were also people from ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit didn't exist. Dusan Latas made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So now your testimony is that not only did Bogdan Grba, your superior in the attack on Saborsko, but also Dusan Latas, the commander of the regular police in Plaski, they both were mistaken when they thought that there was a special purpose unit of the SAO Krajina police in November of 1991. Is that really your testimony, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is my testimony. Nobody can prove that this unit existed. Do you have a list? Do you know who was in command of the unit, where they were billeted? It only existed in stories circulated by people. I would like for somebody to show me a document proving where it was headquartered, who was its commander, who were the members. It says here that it was 15 men strong. That's precisely what I said, that there was a group that refused to integrate into the TO system, and then they waged a war on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. So now -- I'm sorry. So now your testimony is that this group that's referred to in this paragraph of this document by Dusan Latas, that he is saying that he was reinforced in that operation by a renegade group that was not under anybody's command? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's too strong a word, "renegade group." These people were volunteers. They were individual players, if I can call them that. They wandered from one unit to the next one. We didn't still have a firm unit structure at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You referred to them as "renegades" when you were asked by the Defence counsel just a few minutes ago, sir. You used exactly the same term. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did I use the term "renegade"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, that's what was translated to us in English, exactly that term, "renegade."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember using that term. I said that they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I remember. I remember. I'm telling you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's at page --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case I will accept what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It's at page 24.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Look at page 24 on your screen, sir, of today's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure he has the ability to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, okay. He has the screen that's not controllable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can read it, if you'd like, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please read it, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This was in response to a question, actually, from me. The question was: "Q. And it's your testimony that Mr. Grba, in November of 1991, referred to a unit that, according to your testimony, did not exist and had not existed since September of 1991. Is that your testimony, sir?" And your answer was: "A. Yes. That former unit, apart from the renegade part with Rade Milanovic, entered the composition of the regular and reserve police force."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that. Your Honours, you said that I said this to Defence counsel. That's what confused me. You can check that in the transcript. This is the answer I gave to the Prosecutor, and this is what confused me. But, yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then you accept that you used the word "renegade" yourself, and that's how you referred to them. Do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then don't say the Prosecutor is using too harsh a word when he describes them as renegades, because he's taking it out of -- directly out of your mouth. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the Serbian language, that word has a much stronger meaning. It has multiple meanings. This is why I expressed an objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't tell me. You used it yourself, and whatever multiple meanings it has in Serbian, you implied all of those meanings when you used it. So when he uses it, he's perfectly entitled to because he is taking it out of your mouth, irrespective of what it means. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I accept this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Could I just ask a question or two under this head. Now, this renegade unit, you are saying that it did not exist officially, when you say it did not exist? Because there would, on the face of it, be some discrepancy. You're saying at once that it did not exist and then you are also describing it as a renegade unit, whatever that term implies in your mind or imports in your mind.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to explain. Officially that unit was disbanded and it became part of TO units, part of the unit, that is, the unit which, prior to being disbanded, was 40 men strong. Some of them became TO brigade members and some of them joined the regular police. And then there were still some people who refused to accept the new command and the transfer; I called them renegades. However, their number never exceeded ten. These were people who went into hiding at the time. They disobeyed. They didn't want to respond to the mobilisation call and join the TO, yet they didn't meet the requirements to become regular police members, because some had prior convictions, some were alcoholics, and as such they could not become members of police force. Weapons were available to everyone during war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: So the "official powers" that be, in inverted commas, would have been aware of their existence, then, as a unit and as a group, functioning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're referring to official powers, I was the president of the municipality at the time. I knew that they were in hiding and that they acted on their own. They didn't have headquarters; they didn't have a command; they were not part of the system. And their numbers decreased on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: When you say they "acted," what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that they were walking in town in uniforms and under arms, that is to say, they were not where they were supposed to be on defence lines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: What steps, if any, did you take to bring this situation to an end, to curtail and stop it, knowing that the function was outside of the regular system, according to you, and was not lawful?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We finally dealt with such groups, or rather that group, when the military police was established, when our TO brigade became a JNA brigade. That was in late November. Prior to that, we attempted to talk to them individually. I personally talked to them several times. And at that time they critisised me for betraying that unit. It is very difficult to deal with such people without some enforcement mechanism. I had many duties. I had to deal with defence issues, and I didn't have all the time in the world to deal with these five or six men. And they did not represent such a huge danger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why is the number of these people changing so rapidly? You know, there were 15, then there were not more than 10, then there were five or six. What is actually happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's precisely what was happening. Your Honour, whoever was dissatisfied with the assignment he received within the TO unit would go into hiding, become a member of that unit, declare himself to be a special -- specialist soldier, and so on. And their main occupation was to loot Serbian houses. No Croatian houses or households existed there at the time. I had a personal conflict with several of them, and most of them got killed in events that had nothing to do with the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Mr. Whiting at this stage I ask you to proceed, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of them -- Your Honour, by your leave. One of them even went back to the Croatian side. His name was Marinko Mudric. He went to Josipdol wearing a uniform. He crossed to the Croatian side and then he stepped on a trip-wire mine. He was one of the renegades.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will have more questions about this group, which we have now agreed is going to be called the renegades, but I think it is a convenient time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. We will take a break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I just have a few more questions about these men that we've described as renegades. Just to be clear, these men were never part of the special purpose unit of the SAO Krajina police that you commanded, were they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The unit itself comprised people who had gone through training. However, we had losses and the unit had to be reinforced. Mostly those were people who had come from other parts of Croatia. Some were from Ogulin; some were from Josipdol. We had accommodation in the school building, and they had no housing. So we took in some ten people, without conducting extensive background checks. We had no resources to do that. And these are precisely the people that caused the most trouble.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The question was: They were never part of the special purpose unit, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were part of my unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And these are the men that you described as having had prior convictions and some of them were alcoholics and they could not become members of the police force. Are these the same men that were part of your special purpose unit?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, for a brief period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: For how long --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was after the first combat from the 22nd of July to a month -- a month and a half at the most. I didn't have records for these people, and until I saw them in action, I couldn't know much about them. And the unit was established on a voluntary basis. Those who had gone to training with me and who were from Plaski were the people that I knew well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: These ten men who had prior convictions and were alcoholics, did they go to Golubic for training?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's precisely what I said when I started answering your first question. The unit had losses. We had casualties, people who were wounded or killed, so we had to bring in new men. And the reinforcement was on a voluntary basis, and I explained to you what was the reason for people coming from other parts of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And this is -- there was a positive opinion about this unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, when did you have losses? When did you have men killed from your unit? When was that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 22nd of July, Dane Bogdanovic was killed and he was my deputy an commander of the first platoon. Bogdan Cetica was wounded. Following that, Djuro Pesic was wounded, and then some other people fell casualty to mines. Some people got sick. Some people just couldn't stand the pressure. So those were the ten vacancies, so to speak, that were open.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The 22nd of July. Which year, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1991. I've already mentioned that date.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when did you find out that these ten men were alcoholics or had criminal convictions?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the days when they were not on duty, when they had a day off. For example, every ten days they would be given one or two days off, and I could see that they would get drunk during those days, that they would get into conflict with local residents, which was against the rules. They had a tendency to steal; ammunition went missing, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And what did you do about that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disarmed some of them temporarily. I assigned them to do some manual jobs, cleaning and things like that. However, these punishments were of a symbolic nature. I couldn't really discipline them harshly because I needed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you didn't expel them from the special purpose unit. That's how I understand your testimony; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was better for them to be under my control than let them run around freely, because they presented a risk mostly to the property, the property of Serbs, my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please answer the question directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You didn't expel them from the special purpose unit, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just ask one question.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. You were asked, when you discovered that they had criminal convictions and alcoholics, you told us how you discovered that they were alcoholics. How did you discover that, and when, that they had criminal convictions? You told us about them stealing on a day off. That doesn't tell you that they had criminal convictions. That tells you that they were stealing at that time. When did you discover that they had criminal convictions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When talking to my colleagues. I didn't have contact with all of the soldiers, with all of the members of my unit. But these people boasted, they bragged about it. They thought that it gave them an edge, that they had been in prison. There were not many such cases. But once I learned of them, I had these people under firm control. I didn't entrust any important assignments to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My question was: When did you discover that they had criminal convictions? An attempt at answering that question was, when you spoke to your colleagues. I don't know when you spoke to your colleagues. Can you answer the question clearly and directly? When did you discover that they had criminal convictions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In August. This mostly took place in August of 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But certainly by September of 1991, these renegades were not contained in any unit, correct, according to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And they were not -- they did not -- they were not assigned tasks in the military operations in and around Licka Jesenica and Saborsko in November of 1991, were they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They never received any orders from me following that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And they didn't receive any orders from anybody, did they? There was nobody in the JNA or the TO or the police who assigned that group of renegades duties in the military operations in November of 1991, did they?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now you're making me speculate. I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you think it's possible that, given everything you know and your experience at the time and what you observed, you think it's possible that either the JNA or the TO assigned duties in the military operation in Saborsko to that renegade group?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Previously the witness said, "You're making me speculate. I know nothing about that." Now the follow-up question puts the witness under pressure to say something that he doesn't know anything about. I think that the Prosecutor has a right to insist on an argument, but I don't see why he's pursuing this argument further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, I don't think there is an argument here, Mr. Milovancevic. It's just a question. The witness said he would be speculating if he said that nobody gave them instructions. The flip side of that is, is he, therefore, saying it's possible that somebody might have given him instructions that he doesn't know anything about. He's asking about the possibility, not knowledge. That objection is overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Witness, can you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? Which particular portion? I lost my concentration.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The question is: So you think it's possible, given everything you know and your experience at the time in 1991 and what you observed, you think it's possible that either the JNA or the TO assigned duties in military operations in Saborsko to that renegade group in November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it could hardly be the case when speaking of the JNA, and even less of a possibility in the TO. Only those who didn't really know these people would have involved them in something. But, once again, I'm just speculating about this. I don't know of any instances where somebody issued an order for them to do something.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I think your answer is clear. And certainly Dusan Latas was aware of the people in this group; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's go back, if we could, to how we started in on this topic, and that's Exhibit 605. If we could have that back on the monitor. And if we could look at the bottom half of the document, the last big paragraph. You see that paragraph that begins,"On 8 November, 1991 ..." Again, this is written by Dusan Latas, and in the second sentence, he says: "For this task, we received reinforcements of a special purpose unit from Plaski, comprising about 15 men ..." Now, that is not a reference to these men that we've been describing as the renegades, is it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to ask Dusan Latas that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, given your knowledge of the time and given your knowledge of Dusan Latas and what he knew, you wouldn't expect him to write about those renegades in that way, would you? Or to accept to be reinforced in any way by those renegades, would you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that I participated in a military operation and that not everything was the way it's written down here. Maybe Dusan Latas was submitting this to a supervisor, hoping to gain points or to achieve something. I'm a realistic person. I can speak only of what I saw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But you are now speculating, sir, aren't you? You're speculating on the -- sssh. Listen to me. You are speculating on Dusan Latas's motives, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am guessing. I am speculating because I don't know about this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Don't speculate. Give us facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You know Dusan Latas, sir.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you know that he would not refer to the renegades in this report in that fashion. He's not talking about the renegades there, is he?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know why you insist on my answering questions I know nothing about. I don't know anything about Dusan's motives in writing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, one thing, though, you did tell us --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you want, I'll tell you what really happened that day, if you want to hear facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't try to make me say something about things I never wrote down or signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just trying to find out what you know. I will ask the questions, and if you could just concentrate on answering the questions, please. Now, something you told us before is that the renegade -- the renegades did not participate in the military action on Saborsko on the 12th of November, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that they did not participate in it under my command. Over 300 men on our side participated in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, in fact, there were more than 700 men on your side, weren't there?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with that number.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, on the 12th of November, 1991, Dusan Latas was part of your group during the attack on Saborsko; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Well, why don't we look at the next page of this document, then, when he talks about the attack on Saborsko. It's on page 2 of the B/C/S and it's on page 2 of the English, and it's the bottom of the B/C/S. It says there, that paragraph where it says, "On 12 November 1991, following the air attack ..." And then the next sentence says, "There it waited for the artillery fire." And then the next sentence is the one I'm interested in. "The police unit and the special unit made up the right flank of our attack." Do you see that, sir, that sentence? "The police unit and the special unit made up the right flank of our attack." Now, the special unit there is not the renegades because you've told us that the renegades were not part of your group on that day. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with you, but only --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- only in as much as you say that they were not part of that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, he says here, "This police unit and the special unit made up the right flank of our attack." Mr. Latas, when he refers to the special unit, could not be talking about the renegades because you've told us that the renegades were not part of your group. Agree?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, in fact, the reference there to the special unit is to the special unit -- the special purpose unit of the SAO Krajina police, which still existed on that day and participated in the action on Saborsko; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's your construction, and it's not the only incorrect thing in this text signed by Dusan Latas. Could I be allowed to read all of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- because I see things now that are not correct in the next part of the text. You cannot extract things out of context.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, the answer to your question is no. And please just answer my questions and we can move on. Now you have answered my question. I think I'm done with this document for the moment. Yes, I want to ask you some questions -- I'm done with this document for the moment. I want to ask you some questions about the training at Golubic. Well, let me ask you one last question, just to make it absolutely clear. It's still your position that, despite these references in these documents from November of 1991 to the special unit, that the special purpose unit of the SAO Krajina police did not exist. That's still your testimony; right? Just so we're clear.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert that, and I've already spoken about that more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me look at this text. More than half of it is incorrect. I don't know why it's written the way it is. There's some kind of fighting with knives and hand-grenades mentioned here, and that we inflicted huge losses on the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to have an opportunity to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't an action film, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, sir, listen, sir. Can you please subject yourself to some discipline in court. When you are asked to keep quiet, please stop, because you are now telling you us stories which are no answers to any questions put to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We will come back to that exact section of the report, sir. We will come back to it later in your testimony, I promise you. I have some questions about that. Now, let's talk about the training at Golubic. If we could look at Exhibit 622, please. These are minutes of a meeting dated the 14th of June, 1991. Do you see, going down, there is a reference -- number 15, you see there is a reference to Plaski and there's the number "18" after that. Do you see that on the document, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just in case it's not clear from what you've been able to see, this is minutes of a meeting pertaining to Golubic. Were you able to see that at the top of the document? Look particularly at -- go to number 1. It's "Agreement on Further Work in Golubic." Now, if we could look at the second page of the document, please. Do you see there, it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have the second page in English?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. My screen is not working right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you see there -- oh, here we go. If I could just have a moment. Where it says "Plaski," and then it says, "the construction of defensive positions, the blocking of a town, operating with rifle grenade, ambush," those are some of the things that were contained in the training at Golubic for the people from Plaski; correct? Those are some of things you were trained in; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The way you read it out, it's a little different from what I see written down. It says here, "Plaski, obstructing the road, blockading the town, work with a shoulder-held rocket-launcher, ambush."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, we have to work with translations here and sometimes they can be a little different. But the way you have read it in your language, those were topics that were covered in the training at Golubic; correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would take only a day or two, those four things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So the answer is yes, those were topics covered at the training at Golubic.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one of the topics.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. This will really go much faster if you really just listen to the question and just answer my question, okay? Then I won't have to repeat it several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm done with that document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, on the 1st of February, 1992, charges were brought against you in the Republic of Croatia as a result of your role in the attack on Saborsko; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read that in the Croatian press.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, if we could look, please, at document 0151-0788 to 0788A. Do you see that document, sir? If we could scroll down just so we can see the name on it. That's you, isn't it, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's a letter missing in my mother's maiden name. Everything else corresponds. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- for purposes of clarification - I don't know whether this should be seen as an objection - but the Prosecutor said, "An indictment was brought against you for the attack on Saborsko." In the legal system that existed in Yugoslavia and Croatia at the time, a criminal report is the initial action initiating an investigation, and then it is only at the end of an investigation that an indictment is possibly brought. The reason I'm saying this is that the witness's answer was yes, but what we see here is not an indictment, it's a criminal report. This is a police document. It's characteristic of the legal system of Yugoslavia, and I think it's important for our understanding of the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not quite sure why you say all that you have said, Mr. Milovancevic, but we take note of it. Thank you very much. You said you're not objecting. Yes, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could just look at the second page.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, there's another thing here that's not correct in the document itself, if you can bring it back. In the middle of the page where it says, "Did his military service," it says, "No," but I did do my military service in 1985 and 1986.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But this document does refer to you; correct? Despite those errors that you've pointed out, this is a reference to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it says something about whoever compiled this criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, really, if you could just listen to my question and just answer my question. This document is about you. Right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
