utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could go -- on the second page, in the first paragraph, it states -- well, at the beginning, it says, "There are grounds to suspect," and it goes on, and then it identifies you as an organiser, that you led and directed, what it says are, "Chetnik terrorist units in the attack on Saborsko during which civilians were killed, civilian houses torched, property was looted on a grand scale." And if we could scroll down, it says -- it says about halfway down the page, on the English, it says: "In order to commit war crimes against ethnic Croatian civilians in Saborsko, Medakovic, assisted by the occupying army, collected weapons, formed the so-called Martic's police with whom he conducted military training in Knin, and, in collusion with Milan Martic, formed the so-called Territorial Defence Staff." Do you see that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this is, again, in reference -- these are in reference to you; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you were aware that -- you said you learned by the Croatian press that this proceeding or this report had been issued; correct? You knew that in 1992.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I received some excerpts from their newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you are aware, are you not, that in 1995, in August of -- on the 29th of August, 1995, and the 6th of November, 1995, criminal proceedings were held against you in Karlovac related to these allegations. Did you learn that, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've heard this for the first time now from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, could this document be admitted into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this becomes Exhibit 961.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I want to move to events in 1990 and I want to cover these very briefly, sir. You testified about symbols on the Croatian side. It's true, isn't it, sir, that the chequer-board symbol that you referred to is an historic Croatian symbol that dates back hundreds of years. You agree with that; right, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not an expert in heraldry, but I can say that several members of my family were thrown alive into a pit, my maternal grandfather. I have a different opinion of the chequer-board than you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, just tell me, do you know or do you not know that the chequer-board symbol is an historic Croatian symbol that went back hundreds of years? Do you know that or do you not know that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that from 1941 to 1945 it was the symbol of the independent state of Croatia, but I have not studied Croatian history.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you have not answered my question. This is the third time, and this will literally triple the amount of time that cross-examination will take, if this happens with every question. Can you answer my question, please? Did you know or did you not know that that symbol, the chequer-board symbol, is an historic Croatian symbol that went back hundreds of years?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're making me enter into a discussion about the history of the Croatian people. My opinion differs from yours. I cannot agree with what you say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Witness, you are not being asked about any opinion, you are being asked about knowledge. Do you know or don't you know? And if you don't know, the simple answer is, "I don't know." You are not being asked to go into any discussion of history here. If you don't know, just say, "I don't know." If you know, tell us you know. It's as simple as all of that. You either know or you don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that it's the way you say it is, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does that mean, sir, that you believed, you thought, that that symbol was invented by the Ustasha regime in 1941? Is that what you thought?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't think they invented it. I just know they used it, just as the Germans use the Swastika.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You know, sir, that official proclamations from the Croatian side and from the HDZ and in the Croatian constitution of December 1990 all pledged to protect the rights of Serbs in Croatia. You know that, don't you, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Jovan Jovanovic Zmaj wrote a line of poetry about that, to the effect that bad people say nice things but do bad things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Am I to infer from that answer that, yes, you know that the -- that official statements of the HDZ in 1990 and the Croatian constitution of 1990 pledged to protect the rights of Serbs in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because the Serbs had been a constituent nation in the Socialist Republic of Croatia; that was something that was enacted at the second session of Zavno. When the HDZ arrived, the Serbs were no longer a constituent nation. I don't see, if you deny a nation the right to be a nation and reduce them to the status of an ethnic minority, how you can then say you are protecting their rights. That's something only you can say, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, did you ever take the time to read the Croatian constitution of December 1990?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, sir -- sir, you have answered my question. Yes, you did. So when you read it, did you see -- do you remember seeing in the Croatian constitution that the rights of Serbs were guaranteed? Do you remember seeing that in the constitution?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that rights are guaranteed to the Serbs and other ethnic minorities, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- other minorities are listed who are not very numerous, numbering only about 10.000 people. So how can the Serbs be put on an equal footing with them?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So the answer to my question is yes, the Croatian constitution of 1990 guaranteed the rights for Serbs.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My answer is no, not the way you put it. You keep putting things in my mouth that I didn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, you said -- I'm just repeating what you said. "I think that rights are guaranteed to the Serbs." Then you went on to talk about other ethnic minorities. I just want to isolate that part of your answer. So I am only repeating what you said, sir, not putting words in your mouth. The Croatian constitution of December 1990 guaranteed rights for Serbs; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was promulgated by parliament in which there was only one ethnic group, without consulting the other ethnic groups, without consulting the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're asking me whether I read it, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you have not answered my question. The question is: When you read it, did you see that the rights for Serbs are guaranteed explicitly in that constitution; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that. I'm not expert enough in constitutional law to engage in a discussion with you. I felt threatened in such a Croatian state.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So are you refusing to answer the question, sir? I'm not asking about expertise in constitutional law. I am only asking -- you told us that you read the constitution and I'm only asking you what you read.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection. This is pressure on the witness to say something about a highly expert constitutional and political issue. The witness has already given very detailed answers. I think that insisting on this further is simply a play on words in which the Prosecutor is trying to get a reply which he will find satisfactory. This is not a subject matter to which a simple "yes" or "no" answer can be given.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Milovancevic, the witness is being asked about what he read in the constitution, which is a very simple and straightforward question. Your witness just is evading answering questions. From the time you were leading him, I've been saying to him, "Listen to the question and answer the question directly." Your objection is overruled, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do I need to repeat the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you recall, when you read the Croatian constitution of December 1990, that it explicitly guaranteed all rights for Serbs? The same rights as Croatian people. Do you remember reading that in there; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it was not guaranteed explicitly. There are no institutions that would deal with the protection of Serbs, and Serbs were degraded from the status of a constitutional nation to an ethnic minority. So this is how I read the constitution. Perhaps I misinterpreted it, in which case I apologise to the Trial Chamber for my ignorance. But I'm not an expert in constitutional law.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, sir, just to be clear, you're not now -- you didn't tell us what you read in the constitution, you told us how you interpreted it; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are inviting us to assume that you have constitutional expertise, which you are not being asked about. You are just being asked about what you read. And your counsel is objecting that you are being asked difficult questions. You are leading us into those difficult areas. You are not answering what is being put to you. What is being put to you is what you read, not what you understand of the constitution, not what you understand of what you read, but just what you read, what is written in the constitution. You are literate, are you not? You are able to read and write, are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Just answer the question that is put to you. What you read -- and don't give us a thesis on your constitutional understanding. There are as many understandings of that constitution as there may be people interpreting it. That is not what you are being asked. You are being asked what you read. Now stick to the question and answer it directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I will put the question to you one more time. Do you remember reading that the Croatian constitution of December 1990 explicitly guarantees rights for Serbs? Do you remember that? That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand the "explicit" bit of your question. I don't understand the word "explicitly".

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will explain what I mean by that. What I mean is, it says -- it uses the word "Serbs." It says Serbs are guaranteed the same rights as the Croatian people. That's what I mean. You remember reading that, don't you, sir, in the Croatian constitution of December 1990?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Would you agree with me, sir, that in 1990 there were extremists on the Serb side, among the Serb leaders in the Krajina; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that, at Serb rallies in 1990, there would be -- that there would be sometimes people who would dress in Chetnik dress or symbols? They would appear at those rallies. Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you know who established the Chetnik movement and how old it is? I know much more about that than about the chequer-board which, according to you, is many hundred years old.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you are interested in the Chetnik symbols, please ask me. I know a lot about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, one thing that is great about this job is that I get to ask the questions and I get to decide what questions I want to ask. So if you would just answer my question: Would you agree with me that, at Serb rallies in 1990, there would be -- there would be sometimes people who would dress in Chetnik dress or symbols at those rallies? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is a Chetnik symbol for you? Is the Serbian tricolour flag a Chetnik symbol for you? Because that was the symbol most often displayed. You have to put a specific question to me before I can give you a specific answer. Which symbols?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just answer the question directly, sir. You were asked -- he will explain symbols later but answer the question now. Do you know -- would you agree that, at Serb rallies in 1990, there would be people who would sometimes come there dressed in Chetnik dress or symbols? It's either yes, you know -- yes, you agree or no, you don't agree.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's so difficult about answering that? It's taken a whole ten minutes just to get an answer, "Yes." You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you agree with me --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if you permit me. "Chetnik symbols" is a very broad term. I just wanted the question to be more specific. Which particular symbols? Which Chetnik units? Which period of time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any one of those symbols that you know to be Chetnik, any one of them. Some or all of them. Now, you have answered the question. That's fine. Can we proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that in 1990 and into 1991, Serb leaders in the Krajina and in Belgrade and the Serb media in the Krajina and in Belgrade incited fear among Serbs by generalising and exaggerating the Ustasha threat from the Croat side? Would you agree with that, or not?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I categorically refuse to agree with such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We'll come back to that. But now I want to ask you just a few more questions about Plaski separating itself. As I understood you earlier today, you said that Plaski joined the SAO Krajina in August of 1990, and that it joined the municipality of Titova Korenica in December of 1990 or January 1991. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. You just failed to mention that it was done in a legal way, after a referendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm coming to that, sir. But first, before I come to that, you would agree with me, would you not, that Ogulin -- Plaski, before it jointed Titova Korenica, was part of the municipality of Ogulin; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From 1963 onwards and up until then, it was an independent municipality. From 1963 until 1991, it was part of Ogulin municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. You would agree that Ogulin -- well, the Ogulin municipality was approximately 35 per cent Serb, whereas the Titova Korenica municipality was approximately 80 per cent Serb in 1990; right? That is before you moved Plaski from Ogulin to Korenica.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I disagree with the percentage of Ogulin municipality. I think that you failed to include Yugoslavs in that figure, and those who declared themselves Yugoslavs were mostly Serbs, hence the percentage was much greater. As for Korenica municipality, I don't have the facts for 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does the figure of 80 per cent Serb for Korenica sound about right to you, or are you unable to say?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could agree, because I know of some Croatian settlements in Korenica municipality and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the population of Ogulin in 1991 was approximately 28.000, according to the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of the rare issues on which you and I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And would you agree -- I will press my luck and see if we can reach agreement on a few more issues. Would you agree that, according to the 1991 census, of those 28.000 people, 10.000 declared themselves Serbs and 580 declared themselves to be Yugoslavs. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that this census was partially boycotted and that these figures are incorrect. It was conducted in the spring of 1991, when a lot of people failed to cooperate with the Croats who conducted the census and when a lot of people were gone from their villages. I know this for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm just -- I ask this question because of your answer earlier, where you said that I failed to include Yugoslavs in that figure, and that hose who declared themselves Yugoslavs were mostly Serbs. So we're just talking about those who declared themselves Yugoslavs. You would agree that in 1991 there were 580 people in Ogulin who declared themselves Yugoslavs; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak about that because I didn't see the official facts. You have to tell me who published these figures which you are using.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, I'm just --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was it the Official Gazette? Was it the statistical booklet? You have to say who produced these figures. Because if they were produced by the Croatian side, then I think that they were tampered with, especially if they were published in 1991 or 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm really interested in what you know, and you're the one who told us that, of the people who declared themselves Yugoslavs, most of them were Serbs. But are you now unable to tell us how many people declared themselves Yugoslavs?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't. I was not a member of the census commission or election commission, so I can't speak of those figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I won't pursue it, then. Let's talk about the legality of Plaski joining the SAO Krajina. Did I understand you correctly yesterday - it's at page 15 of the transcript - to say that Plaski joining the SAO Krajina was "perfectly legal"? Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my point of view, yes. I'm not an expert in law, but those people who are lawyers and who organised the referendum - and there was a lady here testifying about that - they fully agree with it. And I accepted that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You have to bear with me for a moment. I just lost my transcript. On the -- when, in January of 1991, the SAO Krajina rejected the authority of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior in the SAO Krajina, that you would not say was perfectly legal, would you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was legal. Why are you challenging it? I think it's legal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You think it's legal? What do you mean by "legal"? Legal in what sense? Under what law?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the SAO Krajina at the time had a statute. It did not yet have a constitution. If this was consistent with the statute of SAO Krajina -- once again, I'm not a lawyer. But I know that this was written by lawyers, and some of them were here. So why didn't you ask them about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But from the point of view of the Republic of Croatia, and under Croatian laws and Croatian constitution, it would not be legal for part of the republic -- a part of the republic to suddenly declare that the Ministry of the Interior of that republic no longer has jurisdiction in that area. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the legality of Croatia separating or seceding from a legally existing state, SFRY, we were the ones who wanted to remain in the SFRY and Croatia seceded from the SFRY, and now you're asking me whether it was illegal for Krajina to secede. I can't agree with that. I believe that Croatian secession was illegal, violent and conducted by criminal means.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you believe that about Croatia's secession and yet you believe that the Krajina secession and the establishment of the SAO Krajina was "perfectly legal"? That's your position?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You didn't understand me well. We simply didn't want Croatia to carry us out of Yugoslavia. We were not Croatian dowry. We were a constituent nation in the territory where we lived, and as such, we believed that we had to remain within the SFRY. As for Croatia, it seceded violently. It established paramilitary formations, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- started a war to secede from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir, I wasn't asking you about your position on Croatian secession and what you wanted Croatia to do with respect to Yugoslavia. I was asking you about rejecting the authority and jurisdiction of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior in the SAO Krajina. That was done in January of 1991 and that was not legal. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Was the Croatian constitution legal in view of the constitution of Yugoslavia? And Croatia was an integral part of Yugoslavia at that time. You're a lawyer yourself. Perhaps you could assist us here. How can we fail to abide with the constitution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, as I said, I get to ask the questions here, not you. So please listen to my question and answer my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: I just want to say something as well. Mr. Witness, I know it's a little different in your system, but in this jurisdiction, it's not customary to engage in repartee with learned counsel who is cross-examining you. It is his duty. He may ask you questions. The Bench will stop him when he has exceeded the bounds. I am advising you, because it may be that you don't quite comprehend your role, that you should answer his questions, and I don't want you to be regarded as disrespectful. So could you understand that from now on and respond accordingly. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm extremely grateful.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I will just put the question to you one more time. In January of 1991, the SAO Krajina rejected the authority and jurisdiction of the Croatian Ministry of the Interior in the SAO Krajina and that was not legal; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I will move on. Did I understand you yesterday correctly that, in 1991, a branch office of the police was established in Plaski that had not existed previously? It's at page 20 of your transcript. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said that, in the course of 1990, a police section was established in Plaski by the MUP of Croatia and it was subordinated to the police station in Ogulin. Dusan Latas was appointed its commander. It numbered 12 policemen, out of which eight were Serbs and four were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was done -- that was done by the Croatian Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not sure whether it was called the secretariat at the time or the Ministry. All I know is that people came from Ogulin to talk to us, and various local communes, about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The point of my question was that it was done by the Croatian authorities. That was done by the Croatian authorities; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And that was done in 1990?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When, in 1990, was that done? Do you remember what month?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was summertime. I don't remember the exact month. It's been a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So it was done after the multi-party -- the first multi-party elections; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, after them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And just so we're clear, Dusan Latas is Serb ethnicity; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He was not the first choice. But those of us from local communes in that jurisdiction rejected the first choice, because he was not competent, didn't have appropriate educational background, even though he was a Serb. As for Dusan Latas, he was accepted by both sides, the Croatian and the Serbian side. And before that he worked for the Ogulin municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I want to move forward and talk about the clash at Plitvice which occurred on the 31st of March, 1991. That clash occurred when the SAO Krajina police tried to establish a presence at Plitvice and deployed police there, including even members of the special purpose unit of Knin. Right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. The special unit of the MUP of Croatia tried to take positions in Plitvice. It was exactly the opposite of what you said. The question is, who came on that day, from where. If they, from Korenica, moved away from their homes 10 kilometres and these other people had come from Zagreb, then you have to wonder who truly belongs there. I don't know what you mean when you're referring to the special unit from Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, let's take this one step at a time. Before the 31st of March, 1991, the SAO Krajina police, including members of the special purpose unit of Knin, tried to establish a police presence in Plitvice; correct? Before the 31st of March.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that. I didn't even know that special purpose units existed at the time within the SUP of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So your answer is "I don't know."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is your answer? If you say no, your answer is not "I don't know." What is your answer, then? Is it "I know"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is that this is 50 kilometres away from my place, and that I didn't know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's not an answer to the question. The question is, you either know or you don't know. You said, "I don't know." Is it -- do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that it happened the way that the Prosecutor described it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you don't know, I won't pursue it, then. You testified about four Croatian policemen who were arrested in Plaski on the 31st of March, 1991, by the SAO Krajina police. You testified that they were released the next day, but, in fact, that's not true. They were held for exchange and they were held for several days, held for the purpose of exchange; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There were attempts to exchange them for the captured Serbs from Plitvice. However, we had no facilities in which to keep them detained, so we released them. We didn't have a detention centre or anything like that, so we released them. I think it lasted only for a day or two. And they were not arrested by any Krajina police. I told you that we had a religious, civic rally at the time. We had internal security which was not armed, and it is these people who detained them, or rather they disarmed them. I think that they were armed. There were three of them. They were members of the state security. They had Scorpio make pistols in their bags, and then they had on their belts some ammunition. And the fourth member, the policeman, he had a semi-automatic rifle and another weapon. He also had a shirt with a chequer-board on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So there were four policemen and they were detained; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After the events in Plitvice, the Croatian policemen in Plaski - I believe you said there were three or four at the time - were not allowed to stay in Plaski unless they declared allegiance, signed a pledge of allegiance, to the SAO Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And they all left; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went to the place where they were from, to Saborsko, and this is where they established a police station. I spoke in detail about it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will take a break and come back at half past 12. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you testified that after the 31st of March, 1991, Plaski was "completely cut off." But, in fact, the -- and was cut off from -- by Saborsko. But, in fact, the JNA passed through Saborsko, after the 31st of March into the summer of 1991, almost every day. Right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you, yourself, in May of 1991, you were able to travel to -- from Plaski to Knin with some 25 men, and then there was an additional group of 16 or 18 men who were able to travel from Plaski to Knin and return; correct? In May of 1991.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I explained, we went along forest tracks. We used forest pathways. I'll repeat again --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you were able to go to Knin and return, correct, in May of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, from Vrhovina via Korenica, Gracac to Knin, all this was Serb-controlled territory. It was territory belonging to the SAO Krajina. Our problem was to get as far as Vrhovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did you get there --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- after that --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: How did you get to Vrhovina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Through forest paths, as I said; Licka Jesenica, the Javornik railway station, Rudopolje, Brdo overlooking Korenica, then Gracac and Knin. So the problem was to go from Licka Jesenica to the village of Rudopolje.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, in fact, the train from Licka Jesenica that ran from Licka Jesenica to Knin was still operating all the way until August of 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly it did in May and in June, because we returned from the railway station, got on the train and came back to Plaski. That train did not go through Saborsko. Saborsko doesn't have a railway line. It went through Licka Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it went from -- you could travel on that train from Licka Jesenica to Knin; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And it did not go through Saborsko?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Also, in April, May, June, July, August, you could travel to Slunj from Plaski; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Civilians could not cross the military training ground. Between Plaski and Slunj, there was a military training ground where there was the dislocated command of the 5th Military District. It was closed off with wires and barbed wire and so on, so you couldn't get through. But even then, it was a track used by tanks through the forest. It wasn't a proper road. The tanks would be brought on trains as far as Plaski, and then they would march to Slunj on the caterpillar tracks, using their track. So you can imagine what the track looked like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The barbed wire and fencing that you described at Slunj, that was put up and maintained by the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you, yourself, travelled from Plaski to Slunj, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went from Plaski to Trzic. That's a village in Ogulin municipality, in the direction of Slunj. Along the banks of the river Mreznica [phoen] we went on foot, through forest tracks. I didn't have any kind of transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is this the occasion when you went with the two Croat members of the JNA to Slunj, to see Cedomir Bulat?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was later on. On that occasion I went in a military vehicle from the Plaski barracks. There was a driver, and Bruno and Divica Gaca [phoen] and I were in the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What kind of vehicle was it, sir? What kind of military vehicle?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a green -- we used to call it a Fiat car. It was like a small Jeep. It was used for communications -- by the communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you said that was later. When was that? What month was that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly in October, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And from Slunj you can get -- you can travel to Plitvice without going through Saborsko; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid you're mixing up the Slunj military training ground and the town of Slunj. At that town, the town of Slunj was under the control of the Croatian MUP, whereas the Slunj military training ground, which is between Plaski and Slunj, was under JNA control. After the first open conflicts between JNA and the Croatian forces, the JNA couldn't go through Slunj either. They had to use alternative routes. The town of Slunj and Plitvice are linked by a main road, an asphalt road, but we couldn't use that road because we couldn't enter Slunj, the town of Slunj. The gates of the military training ground were a kilometre or two away from the first houses belonging to the town of Slunj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But, sir, the JNA could use alternative routes to get from the training ground in Slunj to Plitvice; correct? Or do you not know?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the open conflict began after the fall of the barracks in Ogulin - that was in the summer of 1991 - it was between the paramilitary forces and the JNA. Up until August, the JNA had been a buffer zone between the Croatian and Serb forces. But as of August, the open attack on JNA facilities and barracks was launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If you could just answer my question, sir. The JNA could -- regardless of this conflict, it could use alternative routes to travel from the Slunj barracks to Plitvice. Even if it did not use the main road going through Slunj, it could use alternative roads. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no alternative routes, apart from the ones we used from Plaski through Javornik and Rudopolje. There is no other route, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So your answer, your testimony, is that no, the JNA could not travel from Slunj barracks to Plitvice. That's your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the outbreak of the open conflict, which means end of August and September, no, until the fall of Slunj.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's talk about the situation in Plaski in May, June, July of 1991. You've already testified that there was a regular police commanded by Dusan Latas. You were commander of the special purpose unit of the SAO Krajina police, and there was also a branch of the state security or DB in Plaski; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: When was it created?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that it was created, and I don't know who created it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You don't know that it was -- that before November of 1991 there was a DB unit or section in Plaski and that it was commanded by Djuro Ogrizovic? You're not aware of that?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew the late Djuro Ogrizovic and I knew he had several men around him. But I never received in writing, either from him or anyone else, or orally, any information as to who had established that unit and for what purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you -- okay. Let's take this one step at a time. By November of 1991, Djuro Ogrizovic had a unit of men; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One can't speak of any kind of unit. Perhaps it was just a group of men who obeyed him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Let's put that aside for a moment. Do you know anything about a DB unit or section of Plaski being created before -- by November of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could just look at Exhibit 605, please. Again, if we could look at the last full paragraph of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is the same document we've seen before, sir. In the last --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do Your Honours have the English? I'm sorry to keep asking but my LiveNote is not acting properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your Honours have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, do you see there in that paragraph it says -- that begins "On the 8th of November, 1991 ..." and then moving to the second sentence, it says -- this is, again, the document written by Dusan Latas. It says: "For this task we received reinforcements of a special purpose unit from Plaski, comprising about 15 men, while the Plaski DB section acted directly with our unit." This is in reference to the 8th of November, 1991. Does this help you remember anything at all about a DB unit of Plaski being in assistance at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did know about the existence of that unit. I didn't write this letter. You'd have to ask Dusan about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'm sorry, but just a few moments ago, I asked you this question and I said: "Do you know anything about a DB unit or section of Plaski being created before -- by November of 1991?" And your answer was: "I don't know anything." But now that I've shown you this document, you're saying "I do know about that. I did know about the existence of that unit." Or maybe it was misinterpreted. Did you say you did know or that you did not know about the existence of that DB unit?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I didn't know and that you would have to ask Dusan Latas about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: We just had a misinterpretation there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Wasn't there a misunderstanding maybe also due to the use of the word "unit" by you, Mr. Whiting? The witness explained to us it was maybe a group. Could we talk of a group of armed people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I spoke about a group of men gathered around Djuro Ogrizovic, and I said that I knew him personally when you asked me about him. But there was some kind of squad of the state security in Plaski. I know nothing about that. Nobody ever told me about it. I was then the president of the municipality, and nobody ever informed me of the establishment of a squad, as it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look at Exhibit 606, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is a document that's dated the 6th of November, 1991. And if we could just scroll down to the bottom so we could see who it's from. You can see it's from and signed by Djuro Ogrizovic. And at the top, it says: "Of Recognizance Sabotage Squad Special Forces in Plaski within this DB department as follows," and then there is a list of names. Does that help you recollect anything about there being a DB unit in Plaski?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please scroll up so I can see who this is addressed to?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: It just says "List" at the top. No address.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about this list, and I assert that anyone could have written this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And this doesn't -- put aside the list for the moment. This doesn't help you, seeing these names in this document, this doesn't help you recollect anything about the existence of a DB unit or group or section within Plaski at that time?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know most of these people; in fact, I know them all. Some of them are deceased. But I don't know to whom this was addressed. It says here, "According to agreement." Who was the agreement reached with? I really can't say anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, having seen this document, you still know nothing about the existence of a DB unit or section or group in Plaski.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look, please, at Exhibit 603. This is -- at the top, it's addressed to the Krajina SAO MUP, and then it says: "SDB Korenica." It's dated the 13th of November, 1991, and it's titled "Official Note." And it says: "On 12 November 1991, Saborsko was attacked by the Plaski TO units --" no, "Plaski TO, units of the JNA, special sabotage section serving with the Plaski DB, and by the Krajina SAO police." Now, if we look at the bottom, there's just a number, 91-020. Do you know this number to be the code number for Djuro Ogrizovic?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But, by your leave, I notice in this first paragraph that nowhere is a special purpose unit mentioned in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, we're not talking about that right now. We're talking about the DB.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're extracting what you want from the context, Mr. Prosecutor. I simply observed that in a letter signed by Dusan Latas it's mentioned and yet here it's not mentioned, and it refers to the same event on the same day. If that might assist, Your Honours. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It doesn't assist us because it is the Prosecutor's job to extract what he wants from any document. Just go along with him. When your counsel comes later, he will extract what he wants or what you want. This time, it is the Prosecutor's turn, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could just look at the second paragraph of the document, and it says: "It was my honour and task to command a company on the village at axis, the centre line, with the goal of overpowering the foremost trenches which were difficult to take. Also, I led our special forces to remove mines from the minefields, which was executed well." Then there is a reference in this paragraph to: "Djuka Grubor worked with me throughout. He carried out all his assignments as befitted a DB member." Now, it was Djuro Ogrizovic who commanded the company on the village axis, the centre line; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. If we could look, finally, at Exhibit 607, please. If we could look at Exhibit 607, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mentioned Djuka Grubor here. I didn't notice that name on that list which you showed me, the previous exhibit, but I knew that man, too. He's deceased. That man wasn't from Plaski.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. If you could just please focus on my questions, we'll get done sooner. If we could look please at Exhibit 607. And if we could look at page 3 of the English and page 6 of the B/C/S. You saw this document before. This is the handwritten order, written by Bogdan - I've forgotten his name for a minute - Grba on the 10th of November, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Is that page 6 of the B/C/S? If you could just scroll down. I don't remember if it is at the top or the bottom, but I will see it -- I will know it when I see it. I think it may be at the top. Yes. And we're on page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: In the second paragraph, it says: "I company consists of: Special sabotage unit, II battalion 1st platoon and III battalion 1st platoon. The unit is commanded by Ogrizovic Djuro." That's correct, isn't it? He commanded a special sabotage unit, and it was part of the DB. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that. I see here that Bogdan Grba said that this company would be in the attack on Saborsko, but it wasn't a permanent company. You can see that it's made up of different units; it's combined. So you have the first platoon of one battalion and another platoon of another battalion. And that's how I received my order to attack the right side. It's probably in this order, too. It's not a permanent company, it's an ad hoc unit which was extracted from the brigade in order to deblock, or rather to attack the Ustasha stronghold of Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes, I understand that, sir. But during that attack, he was in command among other forces of the special sabotage unit, correct, as it says in this document?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says so in the document. I really didn't see them during the attack. I was quite far from them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And, having seen all of these documents which make reference to Djuro Ogrizovic and the DB of Plaski, is it still your testimony that you knew nothing about the existence of a DB unit or section or group in Plaski in November of 1991? Is that still your testimony?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know on the basis of what I can confirm that. I have no document or paper. I received no such document. I knew all the commanders and officers of the brigades, battalions, the chief of police, the police station commander. I was informed about everything, but I really don't know anything about this. I would like you to show me anything. You seem to have a whole archives, but I don't see --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, sir --

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- anywhere that anything was sent to the president of the municipality, which is what I was at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please, my question was really just very simple. And I just wanted to know that it was still your position that you know nothing about this DB unit. It's really a simple "yes" or "no" question. Can you confirm that -- having seen all of these documents that I've shown you, you know nothing about this DB unit in Plaski in November of 1991; right?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, before you move on, I just want to pose a question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: And it would be in relation to Exhibit 606, I believe, and the names that are set out in that exhibit. Could it be put again before the witness so he could have a look at those names. Exhibit 606. Is it now before the witness? Very well. Now, you were asked about those names and you said you knew the names and some of the persons are dead. To what units, if any, did those persons belong? Or what can you tell us about those persons, having denied that they were members of the relevant DB? Do you understand me, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand you. I'm looking at the names. The first one Milos Momcilovic, if that's the man I'm thinking of, because in our part it is very important to include the nickname because there are at least five men with that first and last name in Plaski. If I only knew the year of his birth --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Please keep it simple, bearing in mind what I've asked you. Don't be expansive. Remember that you told us that you knew the persons and some of them were dead. Think what I put to you and then respond very, very pointedly. We don't want a long, expansive answer. Did you understand them to be members of any units; and if so, which units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Milos Momcilovic was in my unit. He underwent training in Knin. After the special purpose unit was disbanded, he went to the training ground, according to my information. He was mobilised into the JNA. Zeljko Mudric, likewise. Ljuban Korolija is deceased. Predrag Knezevic, I know very little about him. I think he returned to Croatia, if that's the man I'm thinking of. So it's easy to get information from him. Jovo Kosanovic was a postman. He was employed in the post office. Dusko Kompar, I don't know what happened to him. Nikola Trbojevic, I don't know what happened to him either or what unit he went to. Mane Trbojevic was in Knin with me. He was in the unit. Dubravko Vukelic, I can't say anything about him either. Dragan Dokmanovic, I'm not sure which Dragan Dokmanovic this is. I don't want to make a mistake. There were two. Ratko Grkovic was also in the special purpose unit at the beginning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Were any of those two within units that you knew of, the two that you said you aren't sure which one the one listed refers to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dragan Dokmanovic, also known as Zuja, was in the special purpose unit until it was disbanded. As for this list and this squad, I don't know about this. I don't know who this was sent to. I don't know about this list, who drew this up. The Prosecutor could have done this using any typewriter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I want to thank you. But can I remind you again, do not comment on the evidence. It is for the Bench, the Trial Chamber, to reach the findings. Your duty is merely to answer the questions. And you have to learn to do that. You have to abide by the rules of this Tribunal. You must not comment on the evidence, and you have to avoid risking the appearance of being impudent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you suggesting, sir, that the Prosecutor is creating evidence as he goes along which didn't exist? You say the Prosecutor could have typed that on any typewriter. Is that what you're suggesting? Are you suggesting, sir, that this Prosecutor is creating evidence as we go along? Yes or no? Is that what you're suggesting? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I doubt that this document, this particular document is authentic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you suggesting that the Prosecutor is creating evidence as he goes along which just didn't exist, which doesn't come from witnesses? Is that what you're suggesting? Your answer should be either a "yes" or a "no". I don't want to --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm asking you a question. Answer my question. Is that what you are suggesting, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have doubts about this list. I think that it was planted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I'm asking you to answer my question. Will you please answer my question, after that comment, that uninvited comment? What's your answer to my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have doubts about the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Will you please answer my question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but your question is not clear. Would you please repeat it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's very clear. My question is: Are you suggesting that the Prosecutor is creating evidence as he goes along with the case? Your answer should either be a "yes" or a "no." I don't want any further comments on that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, why do you make the allegation that the Prosecutor could have typed this on any typewriter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All of the lists so far and the documents that I have seen here had a clear indication of who they were sent to and by whom, and this particular list here has the following words, "as agreed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: "As agreed" between who and who? Are you suggesting it is the Prosecutor who agreed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, I will read this last line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- towards the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Listen to my question and answer my question, sir. My question, sir, to you is: Are you saying that because you read "as agreed," therefore, it was typed by the Prosecutor? Is that what you are saying? Is that what you are alleging?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that as a possibility, but I cannot categorically affirm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I said, is that what you are alleging sir? Again, your answer should be a "yes" or a "no."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't claim that with certainty, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Why do you make the statement, then, if you can't say it with certainty? You've made the declaration to come and tell the truth here. Why do you make statements when you are not certain of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have objective doubts concerning the authenticity of this document because it doesn't resemble any of the previous documents. It doesn't have the heading showing to whom it was addressed, based on what, and for which purposes. Every document that is an official document has to have its purpose. And as for this one, it just lists the names of 11 people whom I happen to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know where the parties in this proceeding get the documents that they are using here? Were you part of the investigation of this case to know that every document must have a particular heading and not in a particular form? Were you part of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the work that I performed in Plaski, I received documents from police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about your work in Plaski. Listen to my questions. My question to you is: Were you part of the investigation of this case to know exactly where every document came from, to be able to say that this document should not be part of the documents that were collected during the investigation of this case? Were you part of this investigation team?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. I wasn't even hinting at that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, why do you make allegations you cannot substantiate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't make an allegation. I just gave you my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Am I lying, then? I'm lying now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. No, that's not what I said, ever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What are you saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I'm saying is that I don't know to whom this document was sent. I can see that it was signed by Djuro Ogrizovic, but it doesn't resemble any of the previous documents shown to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm warning you for the very last time, okay? You have a very specific role to play in this court. Yours is to answer questions that are put to you. It's not for you to say where documents come from or who could have generated those documents, okay? And you listen to the questions that are put to you and you answer directly to those questions. That's your job. If there's any lack of authenticity of any document, that's the job of your counsel to raise and he will do so at the appropriate time. Yours is to answer questions, okay? I'm not going to hear that again, okay? Because I will hold you in contempt if I hear you say that again. You just sit there and answer questions. Nothing else. If I hear you do something else, I will deal with it. You may proceed, Mr. Whiting.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. That wasn't my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You'd better, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I understand -- what I understood you to say just a moment ago is that you do see this was signed by Djuro Ogrizovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "Djuro Ogrizovic" and the signature is illegible. I'm not familiar with his signature, but the typewritten text is "Djuro Ogrizovic."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, I'm going to move on and ask you some questions about the TO or the Territorial Defence. You testified that the commander of the TO of Plaski was Nikola Dokmanovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, for a long period of time, from the inception to -- I don't know which time, perhaps the establishment of the JNA brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: After the events -- well, let's say in 1991, the TO of Plaski was supplied with weapons by the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: The JNA ordered the members of the TO -- well, first of all, when was that? When were they supplied in 1991? What month?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In July of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And the JNA ordered the members of the TO to burn the crates that the weapons were contained in after they were distributed; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard about that. I wasn't present when they were burned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And uniforms were provided to the TO by the JNA; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to correct you. Most of the conscripts -- rather, most of the people who had a wartime assignment during peacetime had uniforms in their homes. So there was no particular need for the TO people to be issued with uniforms. We had olive drab uniforms. That's how it was organised during the SFRY. Everyone who had served in the army, who had completed their military service, had a wartime assignment in a particular unit. And everybody had a uniform at home, all of those who were, say, under 50 years of age.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Your answer directly is: They were not supplied with the uniforms. Is that what you're trying to say? The question was: And uniforms were provided to the TO by the JNA. Your answer is no? Is that the answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now try to keep it as short -- rather than giving us that long story, a "no" would have sufficed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Having given that answer, if there was any particular reason for a member of the TO to get a new uniform for whatever reason, that person could get a new uniform from the JNA, correct, in 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't speak about that. I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how that functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Fine. In September of 1991, Milan Martic participated in organising brigades in Plaski, Udbina, Gracac; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I don't know what role Milan Martic had in Plaski in organising the brigade there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document - it's document 206 - and just see if it refreshes any recollection on this subject. And if we could look at page 3 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S of this document. As the document is coming up on the screen, sir, I will tell you that this document is a letter written by -- well, you can look just at the beginning, at the top there, but it's a letter written by Dusan Smiljanic to Ratko Mladic, and it's dated the 10th of November, 1994. And if we could just look again now at page 3 of the B/C/S and page 3 of the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting, why do you say it's dated the 10th of November, 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, I meant to say the 15th of October, 1994. Now, if we could look at the -- I've just completely lost everything on my computer here. If we could look at the third full paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The third paragraph starting with "In the period"?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, it will take me a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: This is one of the few documents that I don't have printed out in hard copy, so it's just going to take me a moment to try and see it. It's the paragraph that begins "Given the great opposition and problems in forming the brigade ..."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you see that paragraph, sir? Is it visible on your screen, the paragraph that begins: "Given the great opposition and problems in forming the brigade, especially in the Lika area and part of Banja in September 1991, I organised meetings of the most advanced reserve officers and then representatives of the authorities in Gracac an Vrhovina in which the current president of the RSK, Milan Martic, was present. Following these meetings a brigade was formed in Gracac, Udbina, Vrhovina and Plaski." Do you see that part of the text, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Does that refresh your recollection at all about Milan Martic having a role in setting up the brigades and particularly in setting up the brigade in Plaski?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you read the text where it says that a meeting was organised in Gracac and Vrhovina, attended by the current president of RSK, Milan Martic. Is Plaski mentioned anywhere there? Was Milan Martic in Plaski? The first time he came to Plaski was during a religious holiday when a cornerstone was laid during the renovation of a hall in Plaski. You can read this text yourself and you will see that it doesn't say that he was in Plaski.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, I did read the text and I never meant to suggest for a moment that he was in Plaski at this time or that the meeting had occurred in Plaski. What the text does say is that, after the meeting occurred, brigades were set up in these various towns and villages, including Plaski. And my question to you was: Having seen this document, does that refresh your recollection at all about Milan Martic having a role in setting up the brigade in Plaski? It's either "yes" or "no."

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No role whatsoever did Milan Martic play in the establishment of the brigade in September. The brigade was established comprising the TO staff. It became a TO brigade, that is to say, that a detachment grew into a brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, in that last answer, you said, "No role whatsoever did Milan Martic play in the establishment of the brigade in September." Is the important words there "in September"? Do you know if he played a role at all in the establishment of the brigade in Plaski?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You read a text to me. You ask me about a specific period of time. When I give you a specific answer, then you draw some conclusions that are wrong. I told you both then and later: Milan Martic never played a role in establishing the brigade in Plaski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I warned you a few minutes ago that your role here is to answer questions, not to put questions or query people. Just answer the questions, please. If there is anything inappropriate about the question, your lawyer is here to object and the Chamber is here also to protect you. And if your lawyer is quiet and the Chamber is quiet, you can assume that the question is appropriate and yours is to answer it, okay?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Well, sir, a few moments ago --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Sir, a moment ago, when we started on this topic, I asked you this question: "In September of 1991, Milan Martic participated in organising brigades in Plaski and other towns and villages," and you said: "I can't confirm that. I don't know what role Milan Martic had in Plaski in organising the brigade there." But now you've just told us something different, which is that -- you said, at line 12 of page 85: "I told you both then and later: Milan Martic never played a role in establishing the brigade in Plaski." So which of these two answers is actually correct? That you don't know what role he played or that he did not play a role?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said that this document would help me refresh my recollections and it really did. I remember that Milan Martic, either in September or in July or in November or in any months in 1991, when the brigade in Plaski was established, never played any role.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: What was it about that document that helped -- that caused you to change your answer from "I don't know what role he played" to "I know now that he played no role"? Can you point to something specific in that document that caused you to make that change in your evidence?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to frequently pass through Gracac and Vrhovina, especially Vrhovina. I knew many people from Vrhovina, their brigade commander, and I knew the problems that I had with the group --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you? Once again, listen to the question. What is it specifically in this document - not where you walked past - in this document, that makes you say now you know, changed from "I don't know"? Refer us to something in the document. Listen to the questions and answer them directly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm speaking of Gracac and Vrhovina, the towns that are mentioned in this document where it is said that a meeting of reserve officers and authorities is being organised. I knew the reserve officers and members of -- representatives of authorities in those areas, and I knew the problems that I had with the renegades. And I can tell you that in their area it was a much larger problem. So what I'm saying is that perhaps Milan Martic, as an utmost authority among the soldiers in Krajina, helped them overcome these problems with the names of the units by establishing a single Territorial Defence. Because even 50 years after the end of the Second World War, we still had people being referred to as Ustashas and Chetniks, and especially in Lika. We didn't have this phenomenon in Plaski because I resolved these issues successfully with the TO in Plaski.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So you infer from this document that that's what was at issue in Gracac and Vrhovina?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when you say that you passed through Vrhovina and Gracac, was that in September of 1991?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Both in September and in all months of 1991. I would pass through Vrhovina at least twice a month, and sometimes even more frequently. I knew the chief there. They had seceded from Otocac municipality and they knew -- they had similar problems as we did. I also knew the commander of the TO there. I visited him in his home.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So, when you testified yesterday that, starting in March, March 31st of 1991 and certainly after July 22nd of 1991, that Plaski was essentially blockaded, virtually blockaded, you couldn't leave Plaski, that really wasn't true, because now you've just told us that at least twice a month, in every month, you could go to Vrhovina and Gracac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, sir. I would frequently take those forest tracks, constantly putting my own life at risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Really. Now, the 6th Lika Division was based in Plitvice; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that you have a problem with the museum of the 6th Division which is in Mukinje and the unit called the 6th Division. The headquarters of the operations group under the command of Colonel Djukovic was in this hall, which was called the hall or the museum of the 6th Division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Listen, Witness. If the 6th Division was not in Plitvice, just say "No." Don't give the Prosecutor a lecture in what he should or shouldn't be asking. He's asking these questions. It is not for you to decide his questions for him. Please listen to his questions and answer. Your role is to answer, not to formulate questions. I hope you understand me now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do understand. I just wanted to clarify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, don't clarify anything. I don't need any clarification from you. I'm saying to you now: Answer the Prosecutor's question now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The 6th Lika Division is a unit from World War II. The 6th Lika Division, in 1991 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Listen to the question. The question is: The 6th Lika Division was based in Plitvice. You should be saying "yes" or "no" or "I don't know." That's the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm going to turn to June and July of 1991. During those months, there were busses that travelled from Saborsko to Ogulin; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Up until the 22nd of July, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And when those busses went through Serb villages, such as Licka Jesenica, the passengers -- the busses would be stopped and the passengers would be searched, correct, at checkpoints or barricades or whatever it was called?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified about the clash that occurred on the 22nd of July, 1991, and for my next questions, I would like to look at a map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit 23, the atlas book, page 19, please. I don't know if -- that's fine, yes. And if we could zoom in on the right side -- no, sorry, that's not the right page. I'm sorry, it is page 19, so seven -- page 19 of the book, sorry. You're on page 12 of the book. The ERN is -- 6288 are the last four numbers of the ERN. Yes. And if we could go to the right side and zoom in on Ogulin there. You can see it sort of right in the middle of the page, 19. There.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you just -- are you able to kind of orient yourself on the map? Do you see Ogulin and then Josipdol and Plaski? And just at the very -- oh, no, if we could just scroll down a little bit it will be fine. Actually, it would be very good. Yes, there we go.
