So you can see Josipdol just under Ogulin, and then Plaski, then Licka Jesenica and Saborsko. Do you see all of those markings, sir?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday that, with respect to the attack on the 22nd of July, 1991, that -- and this is at page 36 of your evidence, that the Croatian forces set out from the direction of Josipdol towards Plaski. Do you remember testifying that way yesterday?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And you had a checkpoint at -- you controlled a checkpoint at Vojinovac, which is located approximately halfway -- it's not on this map, but it's located approximately halfway between Plaski and Josipdol; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's near Josipdol, but we can say halfway, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: That's fine. It is closer to Josipdol. And the clash occurred there; correct? That's where the clash occurred. And you resisted the Croatian attack on the 22nd of July, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So that attack had nothing to do with Saborsko, did it? That attack was in completely the opposite direction of Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm done with that map. But nonetheless, Saborsko started to be shelled or attacked by Serb military forces in Plaski and Licka Jesenica starting just after that, on the 5th of August, 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. Yesterday I explained why Saborsko was targeted from the mortar, because of provocations against Licka Jesenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: But I want to focus on the date. It started -- put aside for a moment what you say was the motivation. It started on the 5th of August, 1991, correct, the targeting of Saborsko by mortars?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as a response to provocations.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Now, you testified yesterday that you used the term "Ustasha" in your testimony only after we reached the point in your testimony where we were talking about the three men who had been killed at Glibodolski Kriz, or Glibodol cross. Do you remember that in your testimony yesterday?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I explained that in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes. Can you tell us, please, what does that term mean to you? What does that term "Ustasha" mean to you? What do you think of when you use that term, when you think of that term?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Croatian fascists.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Can you elaborate at all on that? What Croatian fascists? What are you talking about? What does that term mean to you?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I can make a comparison. A difference between a Croat and an Ustasha is the same as the difference between a German and a Nazi in World War II. They're old allies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So is it fair to say that the term -- when you think of an Ustasha, you think of somebody threatening -- who is a threat to Serbs; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, a real threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in fact, long before November of 1991, that term was used widely by Serb leaders in the Krajina and by the Serb media in the Krajina; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only as a response to the rhetoric of the Croatian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Please answer the question. It was used widely by Serb leaders and the Serb media; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: And Milan Martic himself used the term in his public statements, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Milan Martic meant by the term "Ustasha." I know what I mean by it. I cannot comment on his --

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: My question wasn't what he meant by it, my question was: He used the term in his public statements during 1991; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard him use it on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, it was a term that was even used in official military orders and reports, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: If we could look at Exhibit 38, please, and we need -- well, we need to look at page 1 of the B/C/S, and we'll start with page 1 of the English but then we'll move to page 2. This is a document, a TO document, from the SAO Krajina dated the 6th of August, 1991. If we could go to the third paragraph on the B/C/S, and if we could go to page 2 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Do you see where there is a reference to Saborsko there in the third paragraph? If you could just read the first sentence of the third paragraph for me, please.

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "In the course of the morning, fire was opened by our forces on Ustasha positions at Otocac, Saborsko, Sinac, and, according to our information, considerable losses have been inflicted on the enemy."

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So that is referring to the -- to people in Saborsko as "Ustashas," correct, on that date, the 6th of August, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My learned friend is incorrectly interpreting the document. This is a reference to firing on Ustasha positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Those positions are said to be at Otocac, Saborsko and Sinac; is that correct, Mr. Milovancevic? That's where the positions are.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what is said in the report, but reference is made to enemy positions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I can try to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Positions are -- these positions that are referred to are manned by people; correct? That's how you understand the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Sorry, "people" meaning civilians or people generally?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: No, no. I mean people generally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NOSWORTHY
utterances.text: Oh, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I'm not trying to suggest that this is referring to civilians as Ustashas. I'm simply referring -- I'll maybe put it this way: This document is saying that there are Ustashas in Saborsko; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think that is the very essence of the objection, Mr. Whiting. Mr. Milovancevic is saying that this report refers to Ustasha positions. Now, the positions may have been in Saborsko or wherever, but the people living in Saborsko are not necessarily referred to in this report. It is the Ustasha positions. So Ustashas may have come from wherever they came from, took position in Saborsko.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. I didn't mean in my language to suggest that these people in -- Ustashas in Saborsko were from Saborsko. I just meant they were in Saborsko; they were there on that date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: So maybe I will put it this way: On the 5th of August -- well, 5th and 6th of August, 1991, this document is saying that there were Ustashas in Saborsko, wherever they may have come from. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my learned friend -- well, would the Chamber please rule on my objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any answer to the objection before I rule, Mr. Whiting?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: I thought I had rephrased my question to deal with the objection, so I took it that it was perhaps unclear. I agreed that my question was perhaps unclear as it was phrased, and I've tried to make it more clear and more specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you understand why I didn't rule, Mr. Milovancevic? Because your learned friend accepted and rephrased. Then there is no need for a ruling at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOVANCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I've heard that now and I'm satisfied. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Milovancevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. To understand the context, can we go to the first paragraph? Doesn't it speak of "i Ustasha" in Croatian or Serbian? What does that, then, mean, "i Ustasha," in the first sentence of the first paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Where is it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Just above the -- we are on the second paragraph, aren't we, with the Ustasha positions, "Ustaskim polozajima". But there is a first paragraph. Can we start with that to understand the sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Oh, I see. It is the first sentence of the second paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Yes. In the original it's one of the spaced paragraphs. It is the second paragraph, that's true, after one paragraph. There are small spaces and then "U Gracacu u," and so on. You can see that paragraph, starting with "U Gracacu," And the sentence, can you read that and can we get a translation? Can you read that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "In Gracac, in the village of Lovinac, there has been an armed conflict between our forces and the Ustashas."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HOEPFEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I could just -- before we break for the day, if I could go back to my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: You understand this document to be saying that, on the 5th and 6th of August, 1991, there are Ustashas who have positions in Saborsko; correct?

utterances.speaker: NIKOLA MEDAKOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This corresponds to what I said previously when I said that an Ustasha is an armed guard who represents a real threat. In this case, these Ustashas firing from Borik are the farmers from Licka Jesenica who were working in their fields. That's why there was a response.

utterances.speaker: MR. WHITING
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a convenient time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Whiting. This brings us to the end of the day for today. The matter stands adjourned to tomorrow, at quarter past 2.00, in this same court, court I. Court adjourned.
